analysis.one_liner: Bans lead in products made for young children, with a slower phase-in for electronics.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee for nearly two years and the Congress ended before any action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write rules, within 180 days, classifying any product marketed to children under age six that contains more than trace amounts of lead as a banned hazardous substance — meaning it could not legally be sold. Companies making electronics for children would get flexibility: if full compliance wasn't immediately feasible, the Commission would set interim standards to reduce lead exposure and a schedule for full compliance. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in early 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Young children and their families. Lead is a known neurotoxin with no safe blood level for children, and the main exposure routes include toys, jewelry, and other products children mouth and handle. The bill would have removed lead above trace amounts from products aimed at kids under six, and set binding deadlines for electronics that couldn't comply immediately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children under six and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission, within 180 days of enactment, to write regulations classifying any children's product containing more than trace amounts of lead as a banned hazardous substance, taking it off the market.

Covers any consumer product marketed for children under age six, or whose substantial use by such children is foreseeable — a broad definition that reaches toys, jewelry, and other items children handle and mouth.

For electronic devices where immediate compliance is not feasible, requires interim standards to reduce lead exposure and accessibility, plus a firm schedule for full compliance — closing the most obvious loophole in advance.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of children's products — toys, children's jewelry, and children's electronics — would bear the cost of removing lead from their products or their supply chains, and retailers would face restrictions on what they could sell. Small importers with less control over overseas supply chains could face proportionally larger compliance burdens.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and importers would bear compliance costs for reformulating products and testing supply chains; small businesses and importers dependent on overseas suppliers could face the steepest burdens relative to their size.

The bill left the threshold for 'more than trace amounts of lead' to the Commission to determine, so the practical strictness of the ban depended entirely on how aggressively the agency wrote its rules.
The electronic-device provision allows products to remain on the market under weaker interim standards for some period, meaning lead exposure would not end immediately for those items.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: lead exposure in young children causes permanent developmental harm, and children's products were a documented exposure route. The costs fall on manufacturers, who would pass some on to consumers, but lead-free products for young children is a cost that comparable rules were later shown to be manageable. The main design weakness is that it delegated the key safety threshold to the agency rather than setting it in statute.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on February 8, 2005, joined by Reps. Sherrod Brown, Jim McDermott, Juanita Millender-McDonald, and Bobby Rush as original cosponsors.
Twenty-six members cosponsored the bill — 25 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican signed on.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced.
On February 25, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — the last action of any kind in the record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill remained in subcommittee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of children's toys, jewelry, and electronics were better off, since no lead restrictions or compliance costs were imposed during this Congress. Children under six continued to be exposed to lead in products marketed to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Children's product manufacturers, not young children

sides.party_line_note: All 27 supporters — 25 Democrats and 1 Independent — were from outside the Republican Party, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to remove lead from products for children under six, forcing reformulation and supply-chain testing. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran against the public's interest in lead-free children's products.

The bill gave electronics a slower path: interim lead-exposure standards plus a scheduled phase-in to full compliance, rather than an immediate ban. They would still face eventual compliance costs but would keep selling products with lead in the interim.

Banned hazardous substances cannot lawfully be sold, so retailers would lose the ability to stock lead-containing children's products. Compliance would raise costs, though consumers overwhelmingly want lead out of toys.
